::: {#def-if-cond}
#### `if` and `cond`

The expression `(if test a b)` evaluates `test`,
and returns the value of `a` if `test` is true and the value of `b` if it is false.

The expression

```racket
(cond [test1 a1]
      [test2 a2]
      ...
      [else an])
```

evaluates the tests in order and returns the value of the expression beside the first true one,
or the value of `an` if none is true.
Like a function defined by cases in mathematics,
each case of a `cond` applies only when every case before it fails.

`if` and `cond` look like applications (@def-racket-expression), but they are not:
an application evaluates all of its operands (@rem-evaluation),
while `if` and `cond` evaluate only the tests they need and the one branch they return.
`and`, `or` and `define` are not applications either.

:::
